title: COLLINS, David. AN ACCOUNT OF THE ENGLISH COLONY IN NEW SOUTH WALES, from its first Settlement in January 1788, to Augus
description: COLLINS, David. AN ACCOUNT OF THE ENGLISH COLONY IN NEW SOUTH WALES, from its first Settlement in January 1788, to August 1801: with Remarks on the Dispositions, Customs, Manners, &c. of the Native Inhabitants... Two volumes, quarto, two maps, 23 plates, (three coloured) and eight half-page engravings (two coloured), the New Zealand chart with a marginal tear and laid down on fine linen, several plates remargined at the head, a little scattered foxing and a couple of discrete shelf labels on endpapers, with both half-titles, overall a handsome set in fine contemporary speckled calf, rebacked in period style by Aquarius, preserving original labels, London, Printed by A. Strahan for T. Cadell and W. Davies, 1798 – 1802. First editions and extremely scarce. Collins’s First Fleet account is the earliest history of colonised Australia, and contains the most detailed and painstaking of all descriptions of the voyage and first years of settlement in any of the early accounts. The rare second volume was based on Governor Hunter’s papers, supplemented by the official records and despatches. As well, Collins had access to the journals of Bass and Flinders, which he reproduces in detail – this was the only publication of Bass’s journal. Ferguson, 263 & 350; Wantrup, 19-20. Estimate $10,000/15,000

title: DARWIN, Charles, Phillip Parker KING, and Robert FITZROY. NARRATIVE OF THE SURVEYING VOYAGES OF HIS MAJESTY’S SHIPS ADVE
description: DARWIN, Charles, Phillip Parker KING, and Robert FITZROY. NARRATIVE OF THE SURVEYING VOYAGES OF HIS MAJESTY’S SHIPS ADVENTURE AND BEAGLE, between the Years 1826 and 1836, describing their Examination of the Southern Shores of South America, and the Beagle’s Circumnavigation of the Globe. Three volumes in four (including Appendix to the second volume), octavo, with 48 etched and engraved plates and charts (one folding) after P.P. King, R. Fitzroy, A. Earle, C. Martens, T. Landseer, and others, eight folding engraved maps, six text woodcuts, half-titles in volumes 1 and 3 (none called for in the Appendix), occasional foxing and marking, several pencilled marginal notes, the Narrative and Appendix in matching contemporary half calf (rubbed) and marbled boards, all edges marbled, the first volume expertly rebacked, the second with neat repair at head of spine (showing earlier crease), the Journal with a name erased at head of title, in handsome non-matched later half calf and marbled boards, all edges marbled. London, Henry Colburn, 1839. First edition; second state of the third volume, Charles Darwin’s first book, Journal of Researches into the Geology and Natural History of the Various Countries Visited by H.M.S. Beagle. The first two volumes of this complete set comprise the official commanders’ narratives of the proceedings of the two expeditions, 1826-1830 under the command of Captain Phillip Parker King, and 1831-1836 under the command of Captain Robert Fitz-Roy. The Voyage of the Beagle is generally regarded as scientifically and intellectually the most important travel book of all time, providing the evidence for what would become Darwin’s life-long quest to uncover the processes of evolution that has had such a profound effect on mankind in all spheres of human activity. For Darwin, the voyage of the Beagle was “by far the most important event in my life, and has determined my whole career” (Life and Letters 1:61). As is usual with copies of the complete work sold by Colburn from late 1839 the Darwin volume is in the second state with an expanded title and without reference to its being the third volume of the complete narrative. By 1841 at least, Colburn was advertising the King and Fitzroy narrative as available in two volumes, quite separate from the Darwin journal which had been offered separately under its expanded title from at least August 1839. title: FREYCINET, Louis Claude de Saulces de.
description: FREYCINET, Louis Claude de Saulces de. SIGNED, MANUSCRIPT LETTER FROM FREYCINET to Mr Fleurieu, ministry of navy and colonies, regarding the earlier loss of the corvette the Uranie. Foolscap folio, manuscript letter, one page on one leaf (old folds). Paris, 3 Juillet, 1838. An interesting letter from the great navigator, perhaps the greatest of the nineteenth-century French grands voyageurs. The letter relates to the official inquiry into the wreck of l’Uranie towards the conclusion of the expedition. In 1838 Freycinet was finalising the last “partie” of his official narrative of his great expedition in l’Uranie and in this letter he sought a copy of the official judgement on the wreck of his vessel. A pencilled note on the letter by an official indicates that his request had been satisfied. Letters signed by Freycinet are uncommon, especially when they have such a crucial place in the story of his grand voyage account, published between 1825 and 1844. Estimate $3000/5000

title: TENCH, Watkin. A NARRATIVE OF THE EXPEDITION TO BOTANY BAY; with an Account of New South Wales, its productions, inhabitants, &c.
description: TENCH, Watkin. A NARRATIVE OF THE EXPEDITION TO BOTANY BAY; with an Account of New South Wales, its productions, inhabitants, &c. to which is subjoined, A List of the Civil and Military Establishments at Port Jackson. Octavo, a few leaves closely trimmed (slightly affecting the text on pp. 53-4), lacking half-title and terminal leaf of advertisements (although this is not called for by Ferguson), re-inserted in old half calf and marbled boards (rebacked with some restoration). London, J. Debrett, 1789. The first edition: always the scarcest of the First Fleet accounts this first edition is now rarely seen and vastly more difficult for the collector than any of the other First Fleet journals. Tench’s 1789 narrative is the earliest, and arguably the best written, eyewitness account of the first European settlement of Australia. White’s journal apart, the others are more or less official in tone; none has the directness of Tench’s description of life in the first days of the colony. Apart from its importance as the first genuine description of the new colony, Tench’s narrative provides us with the clearest of the surviving images of the first crucial months of settlement. title: KENNEDY, Edmund Besley Court.
description: KENNEDY, Edmund Besley Court. ORIGINAL 1842 FIELD BOOK OF SURVEY NOTES IN PORTLAND (Victoria) AND SURROUNDS. Original manuscript of 223 pages, mainly pencil, with 20 pages in ink, one blank leaf at rear roughly removed, later page numbering neatly added in pencil (showing that one original leaf of text was already lost), original oblong leather notebook, worn and with splits and ink marking, the hinges split, with the label of manufacturer Cowan and Co, Edinburgh. [Portland, 1842]. Kennedy arrived in Portland on 22 December 1840. A young man of 22, and a newly qualified surveyor, he had been placed by Sir George Gipps under the command of Charles Tyers. Their overland trip from Sydney to Melbourne was ten weeks, and the second leg to Portland a further four. They reached a township consisting of “one good house, and six decent cottages, besides a few huts” according to the recently arrived Police Magistrate. There were just over 100 residents, but more than 600 in the district. Kennedy’s field work involved periods of camping while he surveyed the rivers, fixed boundaries of pastoral runs, and performed the general survey work of marking out roads, interspersed with periods in Portland during which he was compiling the maps and office work. His field notebook records over twenty separate trips, with starting points including Grange Burn, Camp at Mt Rouse, and Peg at Brook’s Creek. While the manuscript entries are largely numerical, at the same time he notes vegetation (banksia and blackwood, good forest land, fine forest land, swampy flats, thick forest eucalypts) and watercourses which he also shows sketchily, as well as noting features such as a ford, bridge, and stony rise. Measurements are sometimes shown in miles, and a list shows “the bearings of the following hills... taken from Mt. Bainbrigge on a very squally day– Mt. Napier, Mt. Pierrepoint, Mt. Sturgeon, Mt. Abrupt, Mt. Victoria, High Point of Dundas, Sugarloaf of Mt. Dundas, Mt. Eckersley.” Cameron’s hut, Kennedy’s hut and Patterson’s station on the Grange are all mentioned. Only one date is noted: Camp at Marked Tree on Grange Burn for Variations, 7th April 1842. Estimate $10,000/15,000 Lot 21

title: KENNEDY, Edmund Besley Court.
description: KENNEDY, Edmund Besley Court. Sir Thomas MITCHELL. KENNEDY’S ORIGINAL 1846 FIELD BOOK OF SURVEY NOTES as Second-in-Command on Mitchell’s fourth expedition. Original pencil manuscript of 184 pages, 34 of which are overwritten with unrelated subsequent ink notes and sketches, later page numbering neatly added in pencil by Beale, original oblong leather notebook approximately 11 x 18 cms, rubbed and with some loss of surface including the spine, with repaired metal clasp [with] an accompanying notebook. In 1843 the colonial government proposed an expedition to discover an overland route to the settlement at Port Essington on the north coast, which had been established in 1838 as a trading port. In 1845 Mitchell was given command of an expedition and he set out in December with Edmund Kennedy as second-in-command. Over the next twelve months Mitchell explored a vast area of unknown country in tropical Queensland, returning to Sydney on 29 December 1846. Mitchell did not find an overland route to Port Essington and seemed more intent on discovering the great north flowing river he still obstinately believed in. Needless to say he found none, although he represented the “Victoria” as his imagined river in the published account of the expedition. Mitchell’s “Victoria” was in fact the Barcoo and not, as he too hastily concluded, the headwaters of the Victoria River which Stokes had recently discovered flowing into the sea on the north coast. This notebook of Kennedy’s starts on 7 April 1846 “from Peg at Camp 1, no. 4 on a Creek abt 1 mile west of the Balonne”. The pencilled text is mainly measurements, sometimes a bit faint, with notes of vegetation and natural features: myall scrub, white gum forest, pines with iron bark, sand, swamps: as well as numbering of some of the party’s camps, including a reference to “Sir T’s 1st Camp”, and some topographical indications. There is no stated end date, and it seems likely that the text starting on 7 April is actually a continuation from the accompanying second notebook of 175 pages in identical format. This second book has faint survey entries on only around 20 of its pages, the balance appearing to be erased before being overwritten with subsequent study notes of Latin translation, arithmetic calculations, and scribble; later page numbering neatly added in pencil by Beale: the outer board bears the just legible inked name of a young E.H. Turner, Wollongong. Estimate $8000/12,000 Lot 22 page 2 Lot 22 page 3

title: KENNEDY, Edmund Besley Court.
description: KENNEDY, Edmund Besley Court. Sir Thomas MITCHELL. ORIGINAL LETTER TO Mrs SARAH TURNER FROM EDMUND KENNEDY on his expedition as second-in-command under Sir Thomas Mitchell. 3 pages on one folded sheet, small quarto, ink holograph, old folds and splits, the paper cropped under the signature. Camp on the Bogan, 25 December, 1845. Interesting letter from Edmund Kennedy in the field to his Sydney landlady Mrs Sarah Turner: “since we left Boree everything has gone on most smoothly. Sir Thomas has not positively found one fault and interferes in nothing but the course of our travel”; the temperature is 109 in the tent and with a draught “as if out of a furnace”, the bullocks are panting along “one dropped dead yesterday”. Estimate $1500/3000 Lot 23

title: KENNEDY, Edmund Besley Court.
description: KENNEDY, Edmund Besley Court. MANUSCRIPT JOURNAL of an Expedition to determine the course of the ‘Victoria’ River. Foolscap folio, 119 pages on 60 leaves ink manuscript, some sections loosely tied, in fine state. The night before sailing to Rockingham Bay Kennedy wrote “The Rev. W.B. Clarke has offered to send a paper to the Geograp. Society giving an account of my late journey on condition that I let him have my journal to take the particulars from. I think I shall accept the offer.” After Kennedy’s death Captain Owen Stanley asked the Colonial Secretary to see that Kennedy’s journals and papers were given to Clarke. As Beale states, these are the last known traces of Kennedy’s original holograph journal or journals, public or private. “However, Kennedy made a copy of a considerable part of his public journal. This is now in the editor’s possession, and bears signs of hurried work, in that the handwriting is not as careful as usual”. The journal starts on 1 April 1847, and ends mid-sentence on 13 November. This is the text which Beale prints in his 1983 Blubber Head Press work Kennedy, The Barcoo and Beyond 1847, a copy of which is included in the lot. Estimate $20,000/30,000 Lot 24

description: KENNEDY, Edmund Beasley Court. RIVER VICTORIA… CAMP AT DERRIBONG on the River Bogan. 12 January 1848. Foolscap folio, pp. 8; folded as issued. Sydney, W.W. Davies, 22 January 1848. title: TURNER, Alfred Allatson.
description: TURNER, Alfred Allatson. FOUR ORIGINAL MANUSCRIPTS of his journal of the Barcoo expedition [with] two subsequent letters. Two small octavo notebooks, in stiffened marbled wrappers, and two quarto exercise books, the first sewn in original card covers, the second in marbled boards and calf-backed notebook bearing the paper label of Kern & Mader, Book Binders, Stationers, 7 Hunter Strt. Sydney. [Sydney, 1840s]. Coming fresh to the market with a family provenance that stretches seven generations, these manuscripts show the development of Turner’s role in Kennedy’s Barcoo expedition, from field notes to final draft of the journey. The two small pocket books are either field notes or a transcription of them: the first is 44 pages of ink text and 20 pages blank, the second 32 pages of text (ink and pencil) with 32 blank. The working draft shows alterations, deletions, and corrections, the text written in an exercise book of 80 pages (numbered by the author to page 29), the final 16 pages being inserted and loosely sewn. Turner describes the entire journey commencing on 13th March 1847 and arriving back on 7 February 1848. The fair copy generally repeats the draft and is “more carefully expressed” (Beale p. 98). In this text there are wide margins in which Turner has written substantial supplementary detail. Lot 26 (part) Included in the lot are two manuscript letters, the first dated 1st Aug, ‘49, two pages addressed to The Honourable The Colonial Secretary, requesting a tracing of Kennedy’s map “that I was promised … by Mr. Kennedy”; the second undated (the likely date is August 1848, from internal evidence of his appointment as a clerk in the Colonial Secretary’s office) and to an unnamed recipient, six pages foolscap folio signed twice by Turner, a personal account of the country encountered in the expedition, meetings with the existing inhabitants, and the potential for settlement of the region. Estimate $15,000/26,000 Lot 27 (part)

title: KENNEDY, Edmund Besley Court.
description: KENNEDY, Edmund Besley Court. COLLECTION OF RELICS associated with Edmond Kennedy, including three telescopes, a tracing made by him of his map relating to his 1847 expedition, and a related family archive, among others. Includes large antique English brass three draw expanding telescope with leather braiding and dust slides; another small antique English brass two draw expanding telescope with dust slides; and another small antique English brass six draw telescope by Davis of Derby in a plush lined leather covered instrument box. + ‘Plan of E.B. Kennedy’s Return Routes by the Warrego and Culgoa Rivers to the Barwan. Sd Edmond Kennedy, Assistant Surveyor, February 1848’ – fragmented and distressed tracing laid to fine linen (two pieces of fabric joined), 1475 x 580/760 mm. + Silver handled knife and fork (probably French), English sterling silver sugar tongs, English sterling silver salt spoon with family crest, plated silver fork with family crest, carved wooden family seal, leather card case (with Kennedy’s visiting card), silver plate beaker, English sterling silver christening mug (inscribed E.B.C.K., and silk “housewife’’ embroidered ‘E.B. Kennedy’; Kennedy’s signature on a paper scrap, and two miniature books inscribed to Kennedy by his mother. + An antique Swiss pocket watch in an 18ct gold case engraved for King Barton, Kennedy’s friend and executor, and presented by Kennedy’s relatives; an ambrotype (circa 1858) and two copies of a tintype (circa 1885) of A.A. Turner; Sarah Turner’s calling card with her address of 50 Macquarie St.; and some contemporary family correspondence. Preserved in a circa late 1880s Australian pine box. Kennedy’s personal effects reproduced in plate facing p. 68, Edgar Beale, Kennedy of Cape York (Adelaide, Rigby, 1970). On Kennedy’s death, his personal effects came under the control of his landlady, Edgar Beale’s ancestor, Sarah (Mrs Frederick) Turner, née Allatson, mother of Alfred Allatson Turner, Edgar Beale’s ancestor, who was second-in-command of Kennedy’s ‘Victoria’ expedition. Estimate $6000/8000

title: CARRON, William. NARRATIVE OF THE EXPEDITION, UNDERTAKEN UNDER THE DIRECTION OF THE LATE MR. ASSISTANT SURVEYOR E.B. KEN
description: CARRON, William. NARRATIVE OF THE EXPEDITION, UNDERTAKEN UNDER THE DIRECTION OF THE LATE MR. ASSISTANT SURVEYOR E.B. KENNEDY, for the exploration of the Country lying between Rockingham Bay and Cape York; By Wm. Carron, one of the Survivors of the Expedition. To which are added, 1. The statement of the Aboriginal native Jackey Jackey, who accompanied Mr. Kennedy. 2. The statement of Dr Vallack and Captain Dobson, who rescued the Survivors of the Expedition: and 3. The statement of Captain Simpson, of the “Freak”, who proceeded in search of Mr Kennedy’s papers, &c. Octavo, with folding map, with darkened marking of the front board, first blank and map, several leaves roughly opened, with occasional neat pencilled marginalia by Edgar Beale; signed in Sydney in 1849 by Sarah Turner (and again by her subsequently in Wollongong), entirely uncut in original plain thin boards and unlettered green ribbed cloth spine, front hinge opened and the sewing loosening. Sydney, Kemp and Fairfax, 1849. A SUPERB ASSOCIATION COPY of the first edition, signed on the first blank by Sarah Turner, Sydney, 1849 and again on the title-page in Wollongong (now as Sarah Barton). Sarah was Edgar Beale’s great-great-grandmother, the mother of Alfred Allatson Turner, Kennedy’s friend and fellow expeditioner on his earlier 1847-1848 trip to the Victoria River. William Carron’s account was the only published narrative of the fatal Kennedy expedition to Cape York. The expedition was a disaster from the start. Kennedy had been given impossible instructions dreamt up by officials who had no idea of the nature of the country to be explored. When the expedition disembarked at Rockingham Bay it was well equipped, with twenty-eight horses, three carts, a hundred sheep and four dogs. But these resources were less than useless in the country they had to traverse. Rain, insects, leeches and the difficulty in clearing a path through the tropical rainforest slowed the party to a crawl. When it became obvious that the whole party would not reach Cape York in time, Kennedy decided to leave eight members of the party at Weymouth Bay under the command of the botanist, William Carron, while he made a forced march to Cape York with the Aborigine, Jackey Jackey, and three others. A short time after the advance party left Weymouth Bay one of the men accidentally shot himself. Since he was soon too weak to go on, Kennedy decided to leave him and the two other Europeans at Shelburne Bay while he continued north with Jackey Jackey to seek help. Early in December a group of Aborigines to whom Kennedy had earlier given some fishhooks and a knife had followed them. Suddenly they attacked. Kennedy’s gun would not fire and although Jackey Jackey hit one of the attackers and beat them off, Kennedy was struck in the back and leg by several spears, dying in Jackey Jackey’s arms. Over the next few days Jackey Jackey struggled towards safety, dogged all the way by the hostile Aborigines. He reached the shore at Port Albany and attracted the attention of the Ariel waiting there for the party. Even as the Ariel’s boat came to pick him up his pursuers were hot on his heels and he was rescued only just in time. Immediately Captain Dobson of the Ariel set off to rescue the survivors. At Shelburne Bay they were too late. A captured canoe showed evidence that the three men left there had already been killed. At Weymouth Bay they found that all but two men, William Carron and William Goddard, had died of starvation. Here the rescuers were just in time. As Captain Dobson, Jackey Jackey, and two other men from the Ariel broke through mangroves and hostile Aborigines to reach Carron’s camp they found an armed party had entered the camp and were standing with spears poised. Kennedy’s expedition is perhaps the most tragic of all Australian explorations, not least because he and his men were defeated at the outset. The bravery, skill, good humour and generosity of Kennedy, the loyalty and courage of Jackey Jackey, and the endurance of Carron and Goddard all tell of the needless suffering and tragic waste of human life brought about by the ill-conceived instructions they had been given. William Carron’s account was the only published narrative of the expedition, aptly described as “one of the most conspicuous rarities in the literature of Australian land exploration”. Extremely scarce: the official souvenir of the commencement of the work of the Snowy Mountains Hydro-Electric Authority. The Snowy Mountains Scheme was the single most important event in the promotion of mass emigration to Australia since the gold rushes of the 1850s and arguably the most significant demographic event in the history of the continent. Spurred on by the energy demands of the Government’s post-war reconstruction strategy, the establishment of the Snowy Mountains Hydro-Electric Authority was established in 1949 to realise the dream of harnessing the waters of the rivers of Australia’s high country to irrigate the Murray and Murrumbidgee areas and, in the process, to generate vast quantities of cheap electricity. The piece comprises the expected official matter – programme, dignitaries and others, etc. – concluding with an historical and promotional account of the immense project being commenced on pp. 9-31. The fact that virtually all copies seen have been affected by damp is readily explained: “About 4,000 visitors went to the site near Adaminaby in about 1,200 cars. More than 30 Government cars and several buses made the round trip of more than 200 miles from Canberra. The weather was so bad yesterday it was feared that another site might have to be chosen. Rain and light snow made the road leading to the site almost impassable.
